answers.question: the primary source for Last Energy's per-unit PWR-20 price (about $100M) and its 24-unit UK figure (2.4 billion pounds), and any PWR-5 price.
answers.finding: PowerMag's March 2023 coverage of Last Energy's Poland/UK agreements (34 units total: 10 in Poland, 24 in the UK, across three UK site partners) states 'project costs are below $100 million' per PWR-20 unit -- the closest confirmation found of the widely cited ~$100M figure, though it is trade-press reporting, not an exact number published by Last Energy itself. For the 24 UK units, the same article states the deal represents '$2.4 billion' of inward investment in the UK -- in US dollars, not British pounds. The commonly repeated '24 units, GBP 2.4 billion' framing could not be verified in pounds: the article that reports it that way (Data Center Dynamics, February 2026) returned a 403 error and could not be fetched, and every other source checked gives the $2.4bn inward-investment figure in dollars. A separate, much larger figure covers the same UK pipeline: lifetime electricity-sales revenue under the PPAs, reported as 'the power purchase agreement representing over £15.4 billion ($18.9 billion) in electricity sales' -- a decades-long revenue total, not a contract or capital-cost value, and not the $2.4bn figure. Last Energy's own FAQ page (fetched) states no PWR-20 price, no PWR-5 price, and no UK contract value at all; no source checked discloses any PWR-5 price.

answers.question: the primary source for Oklo's stated first-unit cost and its expected $/MWh, and the slide behind the DOE clean-firm band ($63-99 gas with carbon capture, $66-109 advanced nuclear, $69-119 renewables plus storage) that a reporter attributed to an Oklo shareholder presentation. State whether only the reporter's reading exists.
answers.finding: Utility Dive attributes all three figures to Oklo's Q2 2024 disclosures: the $145 million first-powerhouse cost to CFO R. Craig Bealmear speaking on Oklo's Q2 2024 earnings call, and both the $40-90/MWh expected levelized cost and the DOE clean-firm band (gas with carbon capture $63-99/MWh, advanced nuclear $66-109/MWh, renewables plus storage $69-119/MWh) to 'its shareholder presentation.' That presentation is identifiable and public: Oklo filed its Q2 2024 Shareholder Letter as Exhibit 99.1 to an August 13, 2024 Form 8-K, a 26-slide deck. Reading the full text of all 26 slides (including the hidden screen-reader captions describing each slide's graphic content) and grep'ing the raw filing for '$63', '$66', '$69', '$99', '$109', '$119', 'MWh', 'carbon capture' and 'clean firm' turns up zero matches anywhere in the filing. The closest slide (12 of 26) is captioned 'Strategically cost-competitive and highly repeatable' and lists reactor sizes (15 MW, 50 MW, 100+ MW) but carries no cost or $/MWh figures. So for the $40-90/MWh figure and the DOE clean-firm band specifically, only the reporter's own reading could be verified; the primary slide Utility Dive describes was not found in Oklo's SEC-filed presentation. The $145 million figure rests on a spoken quote attributed to a named executive on an earnings call, which is a more solid (if still secondhand) attribution.

answers.question: What does a ton of fabricated TRISO cost, and which vendor's allocation covers its unit count?
answers.finding: Standard Nuclear's July 2026 IPO prospectus (424B4) discloses the first public TRISO price range: 'our current customer order book reflects assumed TRISO pricing of approximately $50.0 - 80.0 million per MTU' (metric ton of uranium). This is explicitly an assumption used to value the order book, not a per-contract negotiated price, and the prospectus does not break it out between the Radiant multi-ton deal and the Antares one-ton deal. The prospectus also discloses a funded backlog of $65 million against a total contract backlog of $245 million and a $986 million qualified pipeline under negotiation. Standard Nuclear's 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 (filed August 27, 2026) does not update or itemize this pricing; it confirms only that Standard Nuclear's fuel-related assets were purchased 'through a Section 363 auction process under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code' from USNC, with no new price disclosure.

answers.question: What does a ton of fabricated TRISO cost, and which vendor's allocation covers its unit count?
answers.finding: DOE's HALEU Availability Program publishes only an aggregate delivery schedule, never a per-recipient breakdown. Its HALEU Allocation Process document commits DOE to 'seek to make available 21 metric tons ("MT") of HALEU' on a schedule of '3 MT by September 30, 2024, 8 MT by December 31, 2025, and 10 MT by June 30, 2026.' DOE's first round of conditional commitments (five of the 15 companies that applied: TRISO-X, Kairos Power, Radiant, Westinghouse and TerraPower) disclosed no kilogram figures, and neither did the third round, announced July 23, 2026, which added NASA and a second allocation to Radiant Industries. GAO's August 2026 report on federal uranium supply (GAO-26-107385) explains why no vendor-to-unit-count mapping exists: it found HALEU 'demands for commercial reactors remain highly uncertain' and separately flagged 'a potential future demand stream for unobligated HALEU to be used as fuel for microreactors under development' for the Department of Defense as still unquantified. No fetched source ties any recipient's kilogram allocation to its planned reactor unit count.

answers.question: Who owns the Global First Power venture after the bankruptcy sale, and will the CNSC application be transferred or withdrawn?
answers.finding: NANO Nuclear Energy Inc. (via its subsidiary Kronos MMR Inc.) now owns Global First Power Limited (GFPL). NANO's press release states it acquired GFPL from USNC on October 22, 2025, with 'the principal consideration paid' being NANO's assumption of 'an approximately $640,000 liability owed by GFPL to the CNSC,' and that NANO 'now directly owns the regulatory licensing application' to build a KRONOS MMR demonstration at Chalk River, continuing from GFPL's completed Vendor Design Review and submitted first part of the licence-to-prepare-site (LTPS) application. This is a separate transaction from Standard Nuclear's $28M stalking-horse purchase of USNC's fuel-related assets in the same Chapter 11 case. However, CNSC's own project page, last modified 2026-01-15 (three months after the GFPL deal closed), still states only that 'CNSC staff have paused all work related to the environmental assessment and the application review for the licence to prepare site as of August 2024' and attributes the pause to USNC's bankruptcy — it makes no mention of NANO Nuclear, Kronos MMR, or any transfer. So ownership has changed and NANO says it is continuing the project, but the CNSC docket itself has not yet been updated to reflect a transfer, reinstatement, or withdrawal.

answers.question: Which vendors is SRC evaluating now, and is the CA$80M still appropriated?
answers.finding: No public source names a successor vendor. At an April 15, 2026 Saskatchewan legislature Economy Committee hearing, SRC's Mike Crabtree told MLAs that over the years working on eVinci, SRC had also identified other microreactors 'both slightly larger and slightly smaller' for different market niches in Canada and Saskatchewan, without naming any of them. Minister Kaeding told the same hearing that Westinghouse redirected eVinci to aerospace and defence work after its own large-reactor contract announcement with Cameco in the US. Neither this hearing nor SRC's own FAQ page (last confirmed updated after the fall 2025 cancellation) states whether the CA$80M appropriated to SRC in 2023 remains earmarked, was reallocated, or lapsed.
